text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Drugs company Astra slumps on the Stockholm bourse after reporting lower than expected sales of ulcer treatment Losec in the U.S. in the first half of 1997. After announcing sales rose 28 percent rather than the expected 40 percent, Astra's share price fell six percent to 147 crowns.

- The Social Democrats want to have higher child allowances and also lower taxes for low and medium income earners, the week's conference at Visby has shown. That is how Finance Minister Erik Asbrink wants to use 15 billion crowns of an expected budget surplus by 1999.

- Less then half of Sweden's students that have applied for university or further education will get a place. Almost 139,000 students are seeking places but only 51,300 will be offered the opportunity.
- Forestry shares rose 1.2 percent on the Stockholm bourse on Thursday, driven up by a strong report from U.S. forestry group Weyerhaeuser.

- The sharemarkets in Sweden and New York keep rising and reaching new highs. Analysts said a good outlook for Swedish companies is giving support to the Stockholm bourse that has risen 35 percent since the start of the year.

- The mobile telephone market is growing quickly and this has boosted aerial maker Allgon. For the first half of 1997 Allgon posted a 37 percent rise in order to 885 million crowns while sales increased by 30 percent to 818 million crowns. The company reported a pre-tax profit of 49 million crowns compared to 33 million crowns a year earlier.

- Cutting taxes by 75 billion crowns could create 200,000 new jobs, according to the Confederation of Swedish Industries, Industriforbundet, which has proposed a new tax system. The confederation put the idea to a politicial meeting in Visby, Sweden this week.

- Swedish students find out on Friday whether they have got a place at university but only one in three are expected to be offered a place. There will be a second chance to get into university or high school with a second round on August 14.

- Sweden is enjoying a record summer with the sharemarket racing to new levels, with turnover 69 percent higher than this time last year, and 1997 expected to be the best year for tourism in 10 years. The number of overseas tourists coming to Sweden is rising sharply and income from tourism is expected to exceed 1995 levels of 116 billion crowns or 3.2 percent of Gross Domestic Product, according to Statistics Sweden. Figures from 1996 were not yet available.

- Despite the tough competition in the mobile telephone market, it is still more expensive to ring from a mobile than from a landline. Average calls from mobiles cost about 3.45 crowns a minute while other telephones cost between 2.21-2.30 crowns a minute.

- Computer company IBS posted a 39 percent increase in sales in the first six months of 1997 to 610 million crowns while its profit after financial items was 20 million crowns. IBS delivers total information systems which includes programmes, hardware and service.
